summary: The web-based IETF email archive search tool, built from the requirements in RFC 6778, was deployed in January 2014. This informational RFC captures requirements for improvements identified during its first years of community use.

plainLanguage.summary: A wish list for making the search box for old IETF mailing list messages work better.

questions: what are the ietf mail archive requirements
how should threads be displayed in email archives
what accessibility features should email archive tools have
subtitle: Making the IETF email archive search tool faster and easier to use.

tldr.problem: The IETF email archive search tool, deployed in 2014 based on RFC 6778, had usability problems: threads were hard to follow, navigation was limited, the interface didn't work on mobile devices, and many features required JavaScript.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC documents requirements for improvements identified by the community during the tool's first two years in use, addressing thread display, navigation, UI responsiveness, mobile support, and non-JavaScript access.
tldr.outcome: The requirements guide development to make the archive search tool more usable and accessible to the IETF community, enabling easier discovery and review of decades of mailing list discussions.

today: RFC 7842 documents improvement requirements for the IETF email archive search tool based on two years of community use. The tool at https://mailarchive.ietf.org continues to serve as the primary way to search and browse the IETF's decades of mailing list archives, and development has aimed to address the usability issues and requirements captured in this RFC.

sections.title: Improving the Email Archive Tool
sections.content:
The IETF conducts most of its technical work via email mailing lists. For decades, archives of these lists have been public, but searching and browsing them was hard until RFC 6778 specified requirements for a modern web-based archive tool. That tool was deployed in January 2014 and has been used by the community ever since.

This RFC, published in April 2016, documents requirements for improvements identified during the tool's first two years of operation. The requirements come from community feedback and represent a concerted development effort to make the archive easier to navigate, more responsive to modern devices, and more accessible to users with different browsers or accessibility needs.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF has decades of email archives. A modern search tool was built two years ago. Now, based on how people actually use it, the community has a list of improvements to make.

sections.title: Thread Viewing and Navigation
sections.content:
When viewing messages grouped by thread, the current tool shows a flat list, making it hard to see where threads start and stop. The requirement is to show threads hierarchically, with clear visual boundaries between them. When sorting by clicking column headers, the sort should apply to the threads first (by the first message in each thread), then sort within threads, keeping threads visually grouped.

Navigation is another major gap. Users should be able to move between messages by date, jump to the previous or next message in a thread, go to the thread's first message, or navigate to replies and references. Currently, the only way to find related messages is to return to the message list and search again. The improvements would add navigation for references (the messages a given message replies to) and follow-ups (messages that reply to the given message), based on the References and In-Reply-To email header fields.
sections.plainLanguage: Right now, a long conversation looks like a flat list with no tree structure. The improvement would show who replied to whom. Navigation should let you jump backward and forward through messages, see the conversation thread, or follow a chain of related emails.

sections.title: Display and Usability
sections.content:
The message list panel can be resized to show more or fewer messages at once, but the control for resizing is not obvious. The requirement is to make this capability more discoverable. There is also a bug: if the display is large enough that all results fit without scrolling, the tool does not fetch additional messages. The improvement would account for the actual panel size when deciding how many messages to load.

The current view has a filter column on the left for filtering by mailing list and sender. This column often appears empty, but it is not clear why. The improvement should explain why filters are unavailable (for example, "refine search to enable 'From' filtering"). Additionally, the view truncates long fields (subjects, email addresses) with ellipses even when space is available. On large displays, these fields should be allowed to expand fully. On small displays, the filter column should collapse or be hidden.

Currently, to get the URI (web address) of a message, users must click on each message in the list individually. The improvements would add a direct link to each message's URL on every row, and provide an export option to download a file containing URIs for all messages in the search results.
sections.plainLanguage: The search results panel should show more detail about messages, like full subject lines and email addresses, without requiring the user to click each one. Resizing the panel should be obvious. There should be a button to grab URLs for all search results at once.

sections.title: Mobile and Accessibility Support
sections.content:
The current archive tool becomes difficult to use on phones and tablets, particularly in portrait mode on smartphones. The requirement is to add a responsive interface that adapts to both large desktop displays and small mobile screens. The filter column, which takes up space on small screens, should be collapsible or hidden.

The tool currently requires JavaScript to function. Modern browsers nearly all support JavaScript, but some users disable it for security or privacy reasons, and some organizations restrict it. The improvement should allow users with JavaScript disabled to search the archive and navigate search results using the message list and single-message views. Not all features (like resizing panels or live filtering) would work without JavaScript, but core search and browsing would be available.

When a user opens a message, there should be hints that double-clicking a row in the list opens the message in a separate window, and a clear way to hide navigation elements if desired.
sections.plainLanguage: The tool should work on phones and tablets, not just big computer screens. It should also work even if JavaScript is turned off, so people who disable JavaScript for security can still search the archives.

sections.title: Administration and Security
sections.content:
For administrators of the archive tool, the requirements include a link from the message view to the administration page when logged in. Administrative imports of messages sometimes need to correct thread indices; the requirement is to automate this correction. Additionally, legacy URLs pointing to older archive formats should be handled with redirects so old links do not break.

Finally, the template used to display messages should be made consistent across all views (message lists, single messages, thread views) to ensure a unified visual identity, particularly that the IETF logo appears consistently. This is a meta-requirement for maintainability.

Security considerations are minimal. The improvements add navigation features which could be used for rapid navigation attacks; implementers should be aware of potential denial-of-service issues if the tool is flooded with rapid requests, as noted in RFC 6778.
sections.plainLanguage: Administrators should be able to manage the tool easily, old links to the archive should still work, and the IETF branding should be consistent everywhere. Rapid automated navigation could be abused, so that needs to be watched.

references.text: Sparks, R., "Requirements for Archiving IETF Email Lists and for Providing Web-Based Browsing and Searching", RFC 6778, DOI 10.17487/RFC6778, October 2012.
